reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Goldman-Cecil Medicine
clinicalPearls: Thiopurines (azathioprine, mercaptopurine, thioguanine) can cause severe, sometimes life-threatening bone marrow suppression
Patients with low or absent thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity accumulate cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides and are at high risk of profound myelotoxicity
NUDT15 variants are an additional important genetic cause of thiopurine-induced myelosuppression, particularly relevant in East Asian and Hispanic populations
Pre-treatment testing of TPMT (and where available NUDT15) status guides dosing and identifies patients needing reduced doses or avoidance
Myelosuppression can present with neutropenia, thrombocytopenia or pancytopenia, sometimes with infection or bleeding
Regular full blood count monitoring is essential throughout treatment, as marrow suppression can occur even with normal enzyme activity
Allopurinol markedly increases thiopurine toxicity by blocking xanthine oxidase, an important interaction requiring dose reduction
Management of established toxicity is drug withdrawal, supportive care, and treatment of neutropenic sepsis or bleeding
reference.pathophysiology: Thiopurines are prodrugs metabolised along competing pathways. One route, via hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, generates cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides that are incorporated into DNA and mediate both the therapeutic immunosuppressive effect and marrow toxicity. Two enzymes divert drug away from this cytotoxic route: thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT), which methylates the drug, and xanthine oxidase, which oxidises it. Individuals with genetically low TPMT activity shunt more drug into thioguanine nucleotide production, causing accumulation and severe myelosuppression at standard doses. NUDT15 normally dephosphorylates active thioguanine metabolites, and loss-of-function variants similarly increase active drug and marrow toxicity. Inhibition of xanthine oxidase by allopurinol removes another escape route, greatly amplifying toxicity unless the thiopurine dose is reduced.
additionalDifferentials: Bone marrow infiltration or primary haematological malignancy
additionalInvestigations: TPMT enzyme activity or genotype before starting therapy
NUDT15 genotyping where available and indicated
Regular full blood count with differential during treatment
Assessment for drug interactions, especially allopurinol
Thiopurine metabolite levels in specialist monitoring
Bone marrow examination in unexplained or severe cytopenias
redFlags: Severe neutropenia with fever or sepsis
Pancytopenia developing after starting or dose-escalating a thiopurine
Concurrent allopurinol without appropriate dose reduction
Rapidly falling counts on routine monitoring
reference.prognosis: Marrow toxicity usually recovers after withdrawal and supportive care, but severe neutropenic sepsis can be fatal. Identifying at-risk genotypes and monitoring counts allows most patients to be treated safely.
pitfalls: Starting standard doses without checking TPMT (and where relevant NUDT15) status
Co-prescribing allopurinol without reducing the thiopurine dose
Assuming normal enzyme activity removes the need for blood count monitoring
Attributing cytopenias to disease activity rather than drug toxicity
references: CPIC Guideline for thiopurines and TPMT/NUDT15
